title: A Discord bot that does one staff job
excerpt: Give a Discord bot one repeated staff job and one owner. Twenty commands and no owner become noise in the server, and the useful command gets muted with the rest.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen. One task, brought to a signature, which is the right size for a staff bot.
caption: One document, one signature. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How do you choose the one job for a Discord bot?
faqs.answer: Look at what staff repeated in the last two weeks, and write it as an input and an output. Routing a request to the right channel, or posting a status the team already trusts, is enough. A clever command nobody has needed yet is not a job. It is a guess.

faqs.question: Who owns the bot?
faqs.answer: One named person, written in the help text, who can change the destination, turn the command off, and explain a bad route. A backup can exist. A committee named as the owner means nobody watches it. When that person leaves, the role moves the same day.

faqs.question: When should the bot be removed?
faqs.answer: Remove the command when the job moves back to email, to the site, or to a different room, and pin one sentence that says where the work goes now. A bot that still answers with last quarter's channel is a trap for new staff. Leave the manual fallback written down while the bot exists, too.

markdown:
A Discord bot for business should do one staff job, with an owner and a sentence that says when it is done. Routing a request, or posting a status the team already checks by hand, is enough. A bot with twenty commands and no owner becomes noise in the server, and then the one command that mattered gets muted with the rest.

Pick the job by counting what staff repeat. If you cannot name the repetition in one line, you are not ready to write the command.

## Choose the job from the week you just had

Look at the last two weeks of the server. Which question did a person answer more than a handful of times, with the same shape every time? “Where do I send this file?” “Is this ticket in design or in build?” “Did the form from the site land?” Those are candidates. A clever idea that has not happened yet is not.

Write the job as an input and an output. Input: a request in a channel, with a link. Output: the request appears in the right channel, with the link and the time, and the original poster gets one reply naming where it went. That is a whole product. Ship that before you add a leaderboard, a joke command, or a summary of the internet.

Give it a name staff will actually type. Short, boring, and the same in the help text and in the channel topic. If the command requires a paragraph of arguments, it is a form, and the form may belong on the site instead of in chat.

One job also means one failure mode you can explain. When it breaks, the message should say it did not route the request, and where to put the request by hand. A stack trace is not a staff interface. A silent failure is worse, because the poster thinks a person has it.

## An owner, a channel, and a source of truth

Name an owner in the help text. Not a committee. One person who can turn the bot off, change the destination channel, and answer “why did it do that” on a Tuesday. If that person leaves, the role moves the same day. A bot whose owner is “the agency” has no owner.

Decide the channels. A request channel, a destination, maybe a log. Do not let the bot talk in every room. Each extra room is a place it can interrupt a client. Client-facing channels should stay quiet unless the job is explicitly a client-facing status, and even then the wording should be the wording you would send yourself.

The source of truth stays outside Discord. The site, the inbox, or the tracker holds the record. The bot posts a pointer. If Discord is down, staff can still find the work. If you store the only copy of a client request in a bot message, you will lose it in a scrollback limit and you will deserve the loss.

Permissions follow the job. Who may invoke the command. Which role the bot is allowed to mention. Whether it may read a channel that contains customer details. Start narrower than you think. You can add a role. You cannot unsend a dump.

The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) frames quality as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, and the guidance is relevant to software people must operate, not only to marketing pages. A command is operable when a staffer can run it without guessing the syntax. It is understandable when the reply says what changed. Put an example in the channel topic. A help command that restates the example is enough documentation for one job.

## What “done” looks like for that one job

Define done before you celebrate the deploy. For routing: a request in the intake channel produces exactly one post in the destination, within a minute, with the link intact, and a reply to the poster. Duplicates are a bug. Silence is a bug. A post in the wrong channel is a bug.

For a status post: the bot publishes the status your team already agreed, on the cadence you agreed, and it includes the time the status was true. It does not editorialize. It does not pull a number from a dashboard nobody trusts. If the status is stale, the owner would rather post nothing than post a lie with a friendly avatar.

Watch it for ten working days. Count failures. If staff work around it, the workaround is the truth and the bot is extra. Fix the command or remove it. Do not add a second command to compensate for a first one people avoid.

Write the manual step on a single card and keep it next to the bot’s card. When the integration fails, staff should not have to remember a ritual. “Paste the link in #build and mention the lead.” The bot is a convenience over a path that still exists.

## Noise is a product defect

Every unsolicited message trains people to mute. Greetings, level-ups, “happy Monday,” and a recap of messages they just read are how a useful bot gets buried. If the job is routing, the bot speaks when a route happens, and when a route fails. That is the whole voice.

Threads help if the team already uses threads. If they do not, a bot that opens threads will feel like a different app. Match the room. Do not use the bot as the wedge that introduces a new Discord habit the same week.

Mentions are expensive. Mention a role only when that role must act. Mentioning @everyone for a status nobody asked for is how the server turns the bot off at the admin level, and you will not be told.

Keep the tone like a careful colleague, not a mascot. Staff tools that joke in the middle of a client escalation make the studio sound unserious. Save personality for places a person chose to be entertained. A routing confirmation can be one sentence.

If a client shares the server, assume they will read the bot. Do not post internal margins, draft feedback, or “this client is slow” in a room the bot might echo. The safest build talks only in staff channels you have audited.

## Build less than the platform allows

Discord will let you ship slash commands for every idea in the kickoff. Decline. One command, one button if a button is truly clearer, and a way to turn it off. Buttons that confirm a destructive action are reasonable. Buttons that exist because the API example had buttons are not.

Do not connect a general chat model to the server “so it can answer questions.” It will answer questions of judgment in the studio’s voice. That is a different, riskier product. If you need a draft, a person can ask a model somewhere else and paste what they stand behind. The bot in the server should be deterministic: same input, same route.

Store tokens outside the repo you share widely, and rotate them if a contractor leaves. The bot’s identity is a credential. Treat it like one. Log administrative changes: who edited the destination channel, and when.

Review the bot’s permissions twice a year, or when the staff job changes. A routing bot that can still manage messages, ban members, and read every channel is an accident waiting for a bad update. Reduce it to the permissions the one job uses.

Hanabi’s stack for product work is the web stack: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and the rest of the site. A bot can be a small service beside that. It should not become a second product with its own roadmap unless you meant to start a second product. Say which one you are buying.

## Tell the team in one note

Write a short note the day the command goes live. What it does, who it is for, the example, and the manual fallback. Pin it. New staff should be able to do the job on day one without a tour from the person who built it. If the note needs a diagram, the command is still too clever.

Include what the bot will never do. It will not reply to clients in your voice. It will not estimate a project. It will not move money. Those negatives belong in the note because someone will ask in week two, and the easy answer in a server is to bolt on a command. The note is how you say no without a meeting.

Review the note when the destination channel changes. A pinned message from a rebrand ago, pointing at a room that is now archived, is a bug. The owner’s monthly pass can be five minutes: run the command, read the reply, read the pin. If those three disagree, stop and repair them before you add anything.

Client work still arrives through the site when the client is not in your server. The form on the marketing site and the command in Discord should write to the same list, with the same fields. Otherwise staff will check one door and miss the other. One list is the whole point of picking a single job.

## Retire it when the job changes

If the team moves the request flow back to email, or the status moves into the site, delete the command and say so in the channel once. Leave a pinned sentence: “Requests go to the form now.” A bot that still answers with last quarter’s room is a trap for new staff.

The next question, once a bot is in its box, is where a model is allowed to help at all in client work. [Where AI belongs in a client workflow](/blog/where-ai-belongs-in-a-client-workflow) is the piece to read next. It draws the line between drafting and the judgment a client will treat as yours.

If you want to see how a studio keeps tools in service of a clear job, browse [Hanabi’s selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The projects are sites and product interfaces with a specific task, which is the same standard a staff bot should meet.
